prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Imagine two people, Alice and Bob, who have never met and who can only talk by shouting across a crowded square. Anyone nearby can hear every word they say. They want to end up sharing a secret, such as a number that only the two of them know, so that they can then scramble their later messages and keep them private. At first this sounds impossible, because whatever Alice tells Bob, the eavesdropper hears as well. The way out was found in the 1970s, and it rests on a simple observation: some jobs are easy to do but extremely hard to undo. Public-key cryptography is the art of building a secret out of such jobs.

The everyday picture is mixing paint. Suppose Alice and Bob agree out loud on a shared base colour, say yellow, and the whole square hears it. Alice privately picks a secret colour, such as red, and mixes it into the yellow. Bob privately picks his own secret, perhaps blue, and mixes that into the yellow. Each then shouts the resulting mixture across the square, so the eavesdropper can see both an orange and a greenish tone. Now Alice takes Bob's mixture and adds her own secret red to it, while Bob takes Alice's mixture and adds his own secret blue. Both of them end up with yellow, red and blue combined, which is the same muddy brown, whatever order the colours went in. The eavesdropper holds only the yellow and the two mixtures, and cannot separate a mixture back into its ingredients. Mixing paint is easy, but unmixing it is, for practical purposes, impossible.

Paint is only a picture, so it is worth seeing how numbers can play the same trick. The numbers version uses a kind of arithmetic that you will recognise from reading a clock. On a clock with twelve hours, if it is ten o'clock and you wait five hours, you do not arrive at fifteen o'clock but at three. We simply count round and start again whenever we pass the top. Mathematicians call this clock arithmetic, and the number of hours on the dial is called the modulus. Nothing stops us from using a dial with twenty-three positions instead of twelve, and that is the dial we will use here. Whenever we work with it, we only ever keep the remainder after dividing by twenty-three.

The other ingredient is repeated multiplication, which you already know as powers. Five to the power of three means five times five times five, which is one hundred and twenty-five. On our twenty-three-position dial, one hundred and twenty-five is five full turns of twenty-three, which makes one hundred and fifteen, with ten left over, so the answer on the dial is ten. That is the whole recipe: raise a number to a power, then keep only the remainder after dividing by twenty-three. This is our version of mixing paint, and it has exactly the property we need.

Here is how the exchange goes. Alice and Bob openly agree on two numbers, the dial size of twenty-three and a starting number of five, and anyone may hear them. Alice secretly chooses a number, say six, and never tells anyone. She works out five to the power of six, which is fifteen thousand, six hundred and twenty-five, and on the dial of twenty-three this leaves a remainder of eight. She shouts eight across the square. Bob secretly chooses fifteen, works out five to the power of fifteen on the same dial, and gets nineteen, which he shouts back. The eavesdropper now knows twenty-three, five, eight and nineteen, but neither secret number.

Now comes the clever part. Alice takes the nineteen she heard from Bob and raises it to her own secret power of six, keeping the remainder on the dial, and she gets two. Bob takes the eight he heard from Alice and raises it to his own secret power of fifteen, again keeping the remainder, and he also gets two. They have arrived at the same number without ever saying it aloud. The reason is that, underneath, each of them has computed five raised to the power of six times fifteen, and it makes no difference to the answer whether you multiply six by fifteen or fifteen by six. Two is the shared secret, the muddy brown of our paint story, and they can use it to scramble their later conversation.

You may wonder why the eavesdropper cannot simply work backwards. Looking at the eight that Alice shouted, could they not find the power that turned five into eight? With a dial of twenty-three positions they could, because the number of possibilities is tiny and they could try every one in a moment. But the real systems use dials with hundreds of digits. Going forwards, raising a number to a power and taking the remainder is quick, even for enormous numbers, because there are clever shortcuts that avoid doing every multiplication. Going backwards offers no such shortcut. The remainders jump about in a way that looks random, so there is no pattern to follow, and the only known approach for ordinary computers is to try possibilities one after another. For a dial of the real size, the number of possibilities is so vast that all the computers on Earth, working for longer than the age of the universe, would not get through them. The security rests on that gulf between the easy direction and the hard one.

This exchange is the heart of what is called public-key cryptography, though it is only one member of the family. The name comes from the fact that each person has two linked pieces of information, a private one that is never shared and a public one that is announced freely. In our example Alice's private piece is her six and her public piece is her eight. A close cousin of this idea, usually called RSA after the initials of its inventors, works like a padlock. Bob can hand out as many open padlocks as he likes, and anyone who wants to send him a secret can snap one shut around a message. Only Bob holds the key that opens it, so the people who locked the message cannot open it again, and neither can the eavesdropper. The mathematics behind that version uses a different hard problem, namely that multiplying two huge prime numbers together is easy, while taking the product and discovering the two primes it came from is brutally hard.

It is worth noticing what these methods do not do. They do not hide the fact that a conversation is happening, and they do not protect against someone who tricks Alice into talking to an impostor instead of Bob. If an attacker stands in the middle, pretending to be Bob to Alice and pretending to be Alice to Bob, they can run two separate exchanges and read everything. To stop this, people also need a way to check that a public number really belongs to the person claiming it, and a whole system of trusted authorities and signatures exists to provide that assurance.

Still, the central idea is remarkable. By exploiting tasks that are easy to perform and almost impossible to reverse, two strangers can build a shared secret in full view of everyone. Every time your phone connects to a website with a padlock symbol in the address bar, a conversation very much like Alice and Bob's takes place in a fraction of a second, with your device and the website each keeping a private number to themselves and agreeing a secret that nobody listening in could ever work out.
